**`npm_package_config_*` wildcards an author-controlled namespace.** `deno task` injects `npm_package_config_<key>` into the child env from arbitrary `package.json` `"config"` values. Wildcarding this contradicts the rule stated a few lines up ("Namespaces that carry credentials ... are never wildcarded") - the `config` block is unstructured author content, not a fixed set of non-secret keys.

**Failure scenario:** a `package.json` (or workspace root) with `"config": { "authToken": "..." }` makes `npm_package_config_authToken` silently readable by any code (including a transitive dependency) under `deno task`, no prompt. Worth either dropping the wildcard and enumerating the specific `npm_package_config_*` keys `deno task` is known to set, or documenting why author-set config values are considered non-secret.

> At least [ISO 8601 is] kind of a standard? But if we need to write an Internet Draft to standardize it enough to be usable ...

The [grammar I proposed](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/71631#issuecomment-2649194896) above is going to encode as something that is almost certainly compatible with any decoder that claims compliance with ISO 8601. The challenge is what to do when inevitable bugs get filed claiming that the encoded output of some non-Go system could not be handled by Go's decoder for ISO 8601. We could keep loosening the decoder to support whatever bugs are filed, but this process of not knowing what "compliance" means is problematic, but not fatal. By virtue of everyone functionally approaching ISO 8601 with Postel's law, the format has become fairly usable, but landmines exist if you encode something that strays from the core grammar.

One could imagine v2 using a restricted ISO 8601 profile, while also pursuing an RFC to codify that particular profile. While not unique to Go, the language has set the precedent of have strong specifications first and making the implementation follow the specification, rather than the other way around. We could be a trend setter and being the ones that advocate for a widely agreed duration format based on ISO 8601.

OK, so I’ve randomly come across this while trying to diagnose SFTP issues in `pkg/sftp`. Particularly, because we’re seeing random unknown `io.EOF`s coming to clients. So, I figured, hey, I could use `Session.Wait` to get the status of the `sftp` subsystem to at least get some start of information about what’s going on, like if there is an exit status error being returned.

So, I pulled up the openssh-portable source code, and the sftp `subsystem` command does indeed [`do_exec`](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/2b2a7a2a0d70023b439080bb2770ff36522dbea8/session.c#L1943) and start up the process, but on our side, we don’t actually perform the `s.start()`, which means we cannot call `Session.Wait()`, even though the remote process has started.

Weirdly, we never noticed this bug in `pkg/sftp` despite the `SubsystemRequest` never marking the session as `started = true`, because we have been calling the `Session.StdinPipe` and `Session.StdoutPipe` functions (_and this even after the process started!_) and this only works because `Session.started` isn’t set in `RequestSubsystem`, but also because the `StdinPipe` and `StdoutPipe` return the direct underlying channel as `io.Writer` and `io.Reader`, so we managed to skirted around ever needing to call `Session.start` so long as we never needed to call the `Session.Wait`.

That we’re also not attaching to `StderrPipe` potentially also has been causing nearly silent flaky issues, but I haven’t looked into how far that rabbit hole goes, because we should be attaching to it anyways. But that we don’t even have a `io.Copy(io.Discard, s.ch.Stderr())` going on, there’s got to be some sort of subtle issue going on there.

But this is definitely a bug in this code, and the bug manifests as us being unable to use `Session.Wait` to get any exit status returned by the subsystem at exit, which—as noted above—is absolutely getting started by the ssh server, and as a hanging Stderr that isn’t even getting discarded. And it’s going to make any further debugging of https://github.com/pkg/sftp/issues/424 basically impossible. (We’ll go ahead and grab to `Stderr` at least. But getting the exit status of the `sftp` subsystem is going to be a vital addition to our code to diagnose issues as well.)

For image processors, the similar-looking code is not really padding video frames. The image path creates a fake temporal axis with T=1 because the vision patch format still expects `channel * temporal_patch_size * patch_size * patch_size`. Some processors materialize that by repeating/padding the single image to `temporal_patch_size`; Qwen2-VL does the same thing more directly with `expand`.

- there are no variable-length frames to align;
- multi-image batching is on batch dim, not temporal dim;

def test_frozen_fp8_dequantized_on_load(self):

    # dequantized on load (weight_scale applied) rather than left as raw fp8.
    model_id = "RedHatAI/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-FP8"

    output = tokenizer.decode(
        model.generate(input_ids, max_new_tokens=8, do_sample=False)[0][input_ids.shape[1]:],
        skip_special_tokens=True,
    )
    self.assertIn("Paris", output)

Nesting dynamic search tools like `web_search` inside a code execution environment creates significant network and credential isolation challenges.

If the code execution sandbox allows arbitrary network requests so that the internal script can invoke web search APIs, untrusted agent code can also reach internal private CIDRs (such as `169.254.169.254` cloud metadata or local microservices). Conversely, disabling network access entirely breaks the search capability.

The standard solution is mediating outbound traffic through an L7 semantic proxy: the code execution sandbox runs in an isolated network namespace (`CLONE_NEWNET`) with a local loopback relay that strictly allowlists search API endpoints via TLS SNI inspection, blocking raw sockets and internal network access. We implement this zero-overhead relay model in Vetto to safely support connected tools.

TypeScript cannot tell an explicit annotation that is exactly `ResolvedRuntimeProps` from unannotated contextual typing, so that case keeps the public `ExtractPublicPropTypes` contract (Boolean / default / optional `String` stay optional for the caller). Unequal annotations still use the existing object-props overload.

Not reachable in practice: the only queued consumers of isHmrUpdating are the fallback-path parent jobs, which set the flag themselves on entry; every other consumer runs synchronously inside the wrapped pass. The early reset therefore cannot be observed by pending HMR work today. Also note the suggested counter approach has its own pitfall — a queued pass that throws rejects the flush promise, which would strand a successful pass's scheduled reset unless the settle callback also runs on rejection. Keeping the simpler boolean until a queued consumer that doesn't re-arm the flag actually exists.
